segments.text: What do these things have in common? Calming down a panicked scuba diver 30 ft under the ocean, treating an overdose at a Taylor Swift concert, and figuring out why the primary application cluster has suddenly started timing out all requests.

Well, they're all scenarios that require excellent incident management, and I know because I've lived through all of those as a dive master and an EMT and an SRE. And the core of good incident management is good knowledge.

All those scenarios demand that you know what's happening and know how to fix it or know how to gather the information to know that. And so today we're going to talk about how we know things. And how do we find knowledge?

And that's epistemology. Epistemology is the study of knowledge. How do we find it? How do we be sure of it? And when the pager goes off and the adrenaline is pumping and we got to wake up at 3:00 in the morning and go fight a fire, vibes aren't enough.

We need concrete models to keep us grounded. Where are we in an incident? To tell us what questions we should be asking and ways to manage our own effectiveness and level of the effectiveness of others to help us arrive at the truth and solve the problem.

And as Michelle in the plenary session yesterday said, with the rise of AI in these systems, they're becoming more and more opaque. And so what that means is that when we get to the point that a human does need to be involved, we need excellent

troubleshooting skills. Now, when I give this talk, I often get a bimodal distribution of feedback. People that say, "Hey, that was really practical and I learned a lot about how to problem solve." And if you're in that camp, awesome. I'm thrilled.

I also get a lot of feedback from people that say, "Yeah, you kind of described how I solve problems." And I'm also happy if you're in that camp because you need to bring these back to your teams. I see so many people go, "Oh, my new

junior like they they don't know what to do when they hit a problem. They just freeze up." You got to teach people. So, my goal is for you to take away a new paradigm, a new script for communication, or a new method for gathering knowledge either for yourself

or to take back to your teams, to your juniors, to your new on-calls, or to other people in your organization that may not even be technical. I give a really similar version of this talk to my EMTs when we're talking about

debugging the human body. The concept of acquiring good reliable knowledge in a crisis situation is really universal. So, let's jump in. This is an incident loop. This is from the Google SRE handbook. I've heard lots of interesting opinions about this book

over the last few days. There are lots of incident loops. There's the OODA loop if you've been around military situations, but the goal of an incident loop is to give us a road map. When there is a crisis, what phase are we in

and what does it tell us about what we should be doing at a given stage. So, we're going to talk through this today and we're going to step through each of these phases and talk about how we manage them effectively. So, the first phase of the zero-with

phase really is the detection and declaration of an incident. And there are so many different practical methods that exist between different companies and different standards, so it's pretty hard to generalize. But in my experience, it boils down to two things

that are universal no matter where you are. And that's codification and teamwork culture. So, codification, write things down. Figure out answers to questions that people are going to have through your incident management process and

literally write a document for a couple reasons. One, so that people know. So that they don't have to pick up based on vibes what your standards and expectations are. But also because regimes change every day. And I'm hoping that the reason you do

things the way you do things is cuz it works. Cuz it's good. And if you don't write that down, if you don't give a standard and a reference that can survive a big influx of new team members, can survive you moving to a different division or you moving to a

different emphasis or moving up in the chain, people can't keep doing the things that work. So what do we need to codify? Codify standards around things like alert fatigue. Alert fatigue sucks, we all know that. Do you have a written

process for how you avoid it? Do you have a threshold at which you will start to look at an alert and go, "Do we really need this?" Is there an escalation method in place so that when someone's on their first on-call shift and they get woken up at 3:00 in the

morning and they look really deep into it and they go, "This didn't need to be a paging alert." Where do they go? Who do they talk to? Write that down. Codify appropriateness for receivers. It's really tempting as SREs to use a

really broad scope and view of the system to take in all the information. As an SRE, I care when my dead letter queue is a standard deviation off normal. John Q product developer, who mainly manages customer experiences, may have

no idea what to do with that. So it's really easy to say, "Well, make good alerts for the right teams." Have you written down what teams should be getting what types of alerts? What archetypes within your role should be receiving pages? Should be receiving

different flavors of pages? And how to keep that appropriate? Codify your severity matrices and your escalation criteria. Nobody wants to declare an incident off vibes. Nobody wants to declare a severe incident off of vibes. And all too often

these severity matrices are done just as a box-ticking exercise to make compliance happy. Hey, we passed SOC 2, we have a severity matrix. All too often there's conflict within the organization. Someone in one corner wrote the severity matrix and some

product manager goes, "Whoa, hey, hey, hey, that's not a severe incident. That's not an SLA impacting event." So, gain consensus on these and write them down so that your on-calls have the criteria they need to make good decisions when the incident happens.

And finally, write down your philosophy. Write down the big picture whys of your operations. For reliability standards, do people understand why we make SLOs? Do they know what the standards are around what constitutes a good SLO? Do

they understand how SLOs interlock with synthetic activation of those SLOs, interlock with post-deployment validation? It's so often that I see beautiful observability and monitoring and reporting systems and I'm like, so why is it this way?

It's just what we build. So, what's going to happen when you're not here to build it anymore? So, write that stuff down. And then a culture of collaboration. It's a critical ingredient in incident response. It's In my opinion, a crisis when there

is one and only one person working on an incident. First, it's lonely. It's scary. This is inherently a high-stress situation and it sucks when you're in it alone. And it is up to the seniors, up to the people who are designing these incident

response patterns to normalize a culture of you don't go alone. If you don't know what's happening, you do page your secondary. You get them online. Yeah, it sucks to page someone else at 3:00 a.m. You know what else sucks? Making decisions alone at 3:00 a.m.

So, normalize asking for advice. Investigate in public. If you see something weird, throw it in Slack and say, "Hey, this seems odd. Can someone come take a look at this with me?" Acting solo is such an enormous amount of pressure, and that consensus, and

that collaboration, and that support keeps that sustainable and manageable. So, let's start digging into an actual incident. The first phase is survival and triage. When the pager goes off, it's so tempting to want to dig in, want to

start solving that problem right away, but there's something we got to do first. We got to keep the boat afloat. We see this emphasis on surviving first in a lot of life-critical situations. In aviation, your three goals, in order,

aviate, navigate, communicate. Your first job is to fly the plane. In medicine, we have our ABCs, airway, breathing, circulation. Does not matter what else is going on. If I don't square those away, the patient's going to die.

So, we need to buy that time. We need to keep the system running as best we can, so we have breathing room to actually solve the problem. So, these can be rollbacks or scale-ups, circuit breakers, cut that traffic right off, access denial, especially around

security incidents, load shifting, if you've got the capacity, failing over, if you've got a ton of capacity. You're looking to buy time in reversible ways to step back from that impinging wall of fire, and be able to have some space to stop and think.

So, we've bought ourselves some time. The house is still on fire, but we are not actively being burnt. We're going to move into the next phase of examination. We're going to gather evidence. We're going to organize our thoughts and our

observations. And the ideal here is to lay down the right information in the right way, so that the conclusion of what's going wrong leaps off the page at us in a a beautiful moment of emergent behavior. That basically never happens.

But, it's a good goal to strive towards. So, how do we set ourselves up for an effective examination? We're going to think in systems and chunks and teach our engineers to do that. It's great to know where all your services are, and it's really important

to have a super super detailed architectural diagram. But, are you teaching people to think in silos, to think logically of I've got my network and edge, I've got my compute and load, I've got my storage systems, I've got my support services and my

upstreams and downstreams, and thinking in those blocks rather than just literally what the architecture diagram is showing you? And this can also be really helpful even prior to an incident because when you look at things this way, it often makes

missing observability chunks really obvious. When you go, "Yeah, well, we have this standard set of alerts and we pasted it all over this application, but if I start drawing boxes here and say this is my compute and this is my administration

layer and this is my storage layer, wow, I'm actually not covering a lot of alerts in that box or between those boxes." So, shifting your perspective a little bit can be helpful to spot those gaps and to spot the problems when you're in an incident.

When we're examining, we need to look at our observability and error reporting, but critically, know its hierarchies. We are mostly SREs in this room. I hope I don't have to tell you, "Look at your Sentry. Look at your Bugsnag and your

Splunk and your Datadog and your ELB logs and your VPC flow logs and your Stackdriver, yada yada yada." Look at those, for sure. I hope I'm preaching to the choir. But, something that so many people miss, especially juniors miss, is the inconsistencies

and what they tell you. If I have a ELB that's reporting, "Hey, I'm getting 504 timeouts from the back end." and then I'm like, "Okay, we got an application issue. Let's go look at Sentry." I have no application error logs that

are reporting any problems in Sentry. For newer investigators or even just in seeking comfort, it's super natural and human nature to go, "Well, let's just pick another information source here. This is inconsistent. I don't want to look at that. Let's go

find something that is consistent." But, that's a mistake. There is information in those inconsistencies. The fact that you've got these two different information sources telling you different things has meaning. Maybe the ELB is going and hitting the

application and the application spinning and the ELB times out and it tries to respond on to a closed socket. Maybe it's getting to the instance, but the instance is so overwhelmed with traffic that my error frames aren't actually making it off the machine.

When you know your error reporting, but critically are teaching people to look at the gaps and inconsistencies themselves, when you understand how those interlock, you can glean meaning from inconsistencies. And you can turn that weirdness into

valuable information. Keep great personal notes. I love note-taking. I'm going to talk about it a fair amount in this talk. Doing that in a public place is great. Stick it in Slack, but you all need scratch pads. I thought, as I got more senior, it's

like, "I'm not going to need notes. I'm going to be so smart. It's all going to, you know." It's the complete opposite. But, great record-keeping's really vital, especially during an incident. This is a note-taking format that I

found really helpful for arranging my thoughts during an incident. We've got evidence of a problem. Why do I think something's wrong? What alerts have fired? What am I observing in the system that's telling me we've got a problem?

What's correlated or causal? As I'm beginning to explore what's part of the issue or other sort of more distant symptoms of the issue or things that I go, "I don't understand how these are linked yet." But, my gut is telling me they're linked. What's normal?

What do we got on the spacecraft that's good? Apollo 13, amazing movie about good problem solving under pressure. Write down what looks fine. One, it rules things out that people have already looked at. Two, they may become

relevant later and having a timestamped piece of information about this was normal at this time can be really valuable. And then what's odd but uncorrelated? I didn't used to have this section in my notes, but I sort of created it by

accident so many times I eventually made it explicit. Computers are weird. Any running system is going to have odd pieces that are doing strange things if you look closely enough. So, make a box for things that you say, "I don't think this is part of the

issue, but it's not normal." And at best, we can maybe follow up in the post-incident review and say, "Oh yeah, we should also go take a look at that." But, those things may also become relevant later. So, really encouraging people to be

taking those good notes, to be taking standardized structured notes, to put hyperlinks in the notes, that are timestamped and that contain that information. This is an example from a real incident I worked a little while back. Under our

evidence, why do I think there's a problem? My Asia-Pacific edge servers are timing out at more than 10% and I've got 500 alarms going off. What's correlated and causal? Synthetics are failing. Great, I've got a local rep route.

I've got logs that show that we're actually seeing that and we had a deploy recently. We're going to talk about correlation in time in just a moment. What's normal? My network edge volume looks good. Here's the dashboard I got

that from. My application logs look fine. Here's the dashboard I got that from. My error reporting looks fine and here's where I got that from. And then odd but uncorrelated, our dead letter queue had a bunch of messages on it. It

had nothing to do with the problem, but we'd started looking more deeply at the system and went, "That's weird." And then like our database had high CPU. As I said, this is a real incident. We never figured out why our database was

hot that day. Just one of those things that happens. So, keeping those notes, encouraging your teams to take those notes and keep them in public. So, we've gathered information. We've arranged it. We've got the things we think we need to

start thinking even harder about what's actually happening. We're going to move into the hypothesizing phase. We're going to come up with a consistent testable theory around what's wrong here. And this loops back on itself. If

we come up with a theory and we test it and it fails, we'll come back to this stage and that's fine. This decision loop, this this uh incident loop, it's non-linear. We can go back. So, what's really key is teaching people how to search.

It's really tempting to sort of overload new trainees on, "Hey, you know, here are all of our systems and here's where you can go and look at the logs." But, have you taught people fundamental models for how to think about a system

and how to step through a system? Can you do a linear search? Basically, like this is what tracing is great for. I could do a whole talk on the things I love and I hate about tracing, but it's great for this particular search

pattern. Just follow a request all the way through. Source to sink. Do a binary search. Bisect your architecture. Pick a cut point. Go between this chunk and this chunk. Are things behaving normally? If yes, I know the problem is

metaphorically behind me in the stack. Move down. Pick a new cut point. Be teaching people these ways to think explicitly. Can we induce a change to learn more? This is kind of a little bit more of a test, but is there something simple and

limited that we can do to give us a ton more information as we're trying to build that theory? Like, you know, can we fail this database over if that's a seamless event? Can we induce a little ripple, toss a pebble in the pond, and see what that tells us?

We're going to think in proximity and correlation. We're going to think about that in terms of time. What's happened recently? When did this start? Does this correlate with anything else that started or fired with it? Are there

scheduled jobs? Is it 9:00 a.m. on the East Coast? Is it UTC midnight and strange mysterious things happen to our application at UTC midnight? We're going to correlate in space. Not literal physical space, but the metaphorical space around your

application. Are surrounding services impacted? Do you have evidence upstream or downstream that's going to point you a lot more clearly to what the scope of impact is so you can make a better theory. And then correlation in action. This is

kind of similar to time, but really looking at the human element. Have we deployed recently? Have we scaled up or down? Have we changed any feature flags? We recently set something up so that any incident room that's spun up immediately gets a

snapshot of all feature flag changes that occurred in the last 4 hours. That's been a total game-changer for us. Don't stop early. I love this quote by Emanuel Lasker, "When you see a good move, look for a better one." Stopping your search and theorizing

early is a terrible mistake. Publish your hypothesis. Yes, and start to chase it down, for sure, but either delegate that to someone and you keep troubleshooting or you chase on that but tag in another engineer to keep the investigation

going. One of the biggest reasons for this is that when there's only one idea in the room, that's the only idea anybody can execute on. And it's not necessarily a good idea. The first thing we come up with often isn't correct and we got to keep

looking. Especially I see this a lot with my new on-call folks. It's hard to figure out what to do when there is no action to take. It's actually way harder when you think you've found something and then it doesn't work because then

you're back where you were except you've got discouragement and failure adding on to your emotional stack there. So, be queued up with those ideas and those theories. Keep looking. So, we'll Let's dig into the epistemology, like the the meat of this.

What makes a good hypothesis? It's two things. It's got to be testable. A hypothesis that doesn't have an action or a set of actions that we can take to prove or disprove that hypothesis is basically worthless. And it's got to be relevant and

specific. This feels sort of self-evident, but it needs to be based on available information. I'm sure we've all been in incident rooms where somebody kind of comes right out of the gate with an absolute wackadoodle theory.

You know, it's cosmic rays. Maybe it is cosmic rays, but we need to have it based on that information, and we need to wrap it tightly around the shape of the issue. It needs to be specific. Something's up with networking is a fine initial thought,

but we have timeouts happening at our APAC edge ingress is much more shaped to the problem and thus becomes much easier to test. And that's where we really start proving things. As we begin to test and treat, this is the meat. So, we've got our

testable, provable theory, and now it's time to prove or disprove it. So, what makes a good test? It's got to work on a hypothesis. It has to actually have something that it's trying to do. And this is really helpful, especially for those new

on-calls, in mitigating that feeling of I need to flip every switch and turn every knob, and oh my gosh, everything's burning, and I just need to do something. You need to have a clear picture of what doing something is going to get you. And

I've been doing incident management a long time, and sometimes even just consciously stopping and thinking, "What am I going to get out of this? What's the decision tree that I'm setting up for myself here?" Actually tells me that the test is poor or that

the information I get isn't valuable. A test needs to favor the likely over the unlikely and the fast over the slow. This is basically if you hear hoof beats, think horses, not zebras. The immediate value of a test should essentially be these two values

multiplied together. If you have something that you think, this is nearly certainly not the problem, but boy, it's real quick just to rule it out. Sure. If you have something you say, look, this is going to burn 20 minutes, but

this is definitely going to fix the problem. That's also great. But if you've got something again, that danger of the only idea in the room, the only idea in the room you're like, I really don't think that's it and we're

going to burn half an hour as we try and do a full redeploy or whatever your long scenarios are, that's probably not a great place to start. Keep looking. Tests need to be mutually exclusive. A positive test needs to prove your hypothesis.

A negative test needs to disprove your hypothesis. Having one of those outcomes or or worse, both of those outcomes not actually give you meaningful information means your next steps are going to be really muddy. And it's a terrible

feeling when you have one outcome that you're like, boy, if this happens, this mystery just got a lot bigger. Those can be valuable for some information gathering, but it's a terrible feeling to basically have a coin flip whether I am going to be

certain of my next steps or completely lost. So, nail those down. A really common place I see this is in tests with compounding factors. You need to have your tests test the thing that they say that they're testing. This is so common with internal

tooling or Dave's special script that he runs. If I say, hey, I think we have a production endpoint that's down. I'm going to hit the endpoint and see if it returns. If it does return, great. We've disproven our theory. But if it doesn't

return, that doesn't mean the endpoint's down. Maybe Dave's script is busted. Maybe I'm not on the VPN. Maybe that endpoint is not reachable from my network segment. So, stopping and consciously thinking about the other things you're

introducing into a problem that you are depending on to go correctly is a critical step to stop and think about. Test needs to be as free from side effects as possible. This one's a pretty easy one. Don't break things. Uh verbose logging is wonderful until

you fry your entire Splunk quota for a month with 1 hour of verbose logging. Uh so, avoid one-way doors. Stop and think. Can we undo this? What are the downsides of this? And a test needs to have clear outcomes and markers of success. Don't move your

goal posts on the fly. It is so tempting that when something doesn't go the way you expect it to, but kind of goes the way you expect it to, to suddenly adjust your criteria of success to feel like that went well. Theory: Turning off this feature flag is

going to eliminate the errors we're seeing. Test: I turn off the feature flag. My error rate drops by 70%. Are we Are we 70% resolved? Was I 70% right? No. You were wrong. Now, don't hear me say that that's not valuable information. That's critical

information. But, it's so easy to scooch those goal posts to go like, "Okay, that Well, that went well. We're just kind of on cleanup." No. Something about the theory you made is incorrect. Something about your understanding of

the problem was wrong. So, you need to consciously take yourself back to those earlier steps, gather more information, come up with a new theory because your prior theory didn't quite fit. So, don't change those goal posts,

figure out what your outcomes are, and stick to them, and derive your action accordingly. Track your results. I'm going to talk about notes again. Data is gold. Even your negative tests, even the things that you went, "Well, that didn't work."

Write that stuff down, and write it down in the open. Put it in your Slack war room. Put it in your incident state document, if you have one. At the very least, keep your own time-stamped notes for a number of reasons. First, you've got to bring

other people up to speed. If this is getting to the point where your tests are failing, there's a good chance you're going to start pulling some more people into that room. They need to know what was tried. What was the outcome?

Second, it's a nightmare come postmortem time. When you are trying to reconstruct what happened during an incident, and nobody wrote anything, it's so hard to figure out what happened when. And especially nowadays, with the rise

of LLM-assisted incident management and analysis tools, they need that information. I won't get into whether I think they're useful or not, but they're definitely not useful if they don't have any actual information to go off of. What was

tried? What's the new evidence that's been introduced? So, track those results. And then, be proactive. I call this time traveling. When you're waiting for a test, when you're waiting to see how something goes, don't just twiddle your thumbs.

And don't get me wrong, grab a coffee, use the bathroom, but don't just sit there. Stop and think about the outcomes of what you are about to do. Imagine that your test succeeds. What's going to happen next? What would you do next? Do you have public comms

that need to go out? Imagine the test fails. What we thought was it the cause wasn't the cause. Who are you going to pull into your war room? What additional logs are you going to gather? Where would you go next? And then, if it's not at cross-purposes,

do it now. Do it right now. The number of times where I'm still waiting to hear back from an engineer about whether something worked or not and I'm drafting up two completely separate public calm statements for if this goes well and if
